::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** two sessions: sections 1 to 6 (80 minutes: Git on your laptop and on GitHub), then 7 to 10 (70 minutes: branches, a merge conflict, pull requests and tags). Boxes marked *Going further* are optional.
- **Slides:** [Git and GitHub](../lectures/04-git/04-git.qmd)
- **You need:** the `ltee-project` from [lesson 02](02-project-organization.qmd) and the [lesson 03 hands-on](03-data-management.qmd#hands-on); Git and a GitHub account with an SSH key ([lesson 00](00-setup.qmd#git-and-github)), or the HTTPS route in [step 6](#put-the-project-on-github).
- **You will have:** your project on GitHub, with a history, a merged pull request, a `lesson-04` tag, and a check from GitHub Actions on every push.
:::

## Overview

Version control records every change to your project: what changed, when,
who did it and why. It lets you go back to any earlier state, try ideas on a
branch without risk, and work with others without emailing files. Git is the
standard tool; GitHub hosts Git repositories online and adds pull requests,
issues and automation (GitHub Actions).

For reproducibility, Git answers the question "**which version of the code
made this result?**". Combined with `metadata/checksums.sha256` (which data,
lesson 03) and `pixi.lock` (which software, lesson 05), it pins down the whole
analysis. Git comes first because everything you make from now on deserves a
history.

### Learning outcomes

After this lesson you can:

1. **Track** a project with Git: stage and commit related changes with clear messages, and keep data and generated files out with `.gitignore`.
2. **Inspect and restore** history: see what changed, and recover a file you deleted.
3. **Use branches** to develop a change separately, merge it, and resolve a merge conflict.
4. **Publish** the project on GitHub and propose changes through a pull request.
5. **Read** the result of an automatic check (GitHub Actions) on a pull request.

Checks: your GitHub repository shows the history, a merged pull request, the
`lesson-04` tag and a green *Reproduce* check (outcomes 1, 3 to 5); the
*Break it* exercise restores deleted work (outcome 2).

## 1. Is Git set up?

```{.bash .run}
git --version
```

Git needs your name and email for every commit. If you did not do this in
[lesson 00](00-setup.qmd), do it now:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.org"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

Use the email of your GitHub account, so that GitHub links your commits to
you. The email is written into every commit, and anyone can read it once you
push to a public repository. To keep your address private, use the *noreply*
address that GitHub shows under **Settings → Emails** (it looks like
`12345678+ada-lovelace@users.noreply.github.com`).

## 2. Start tracking the project

Go to the project and turn it into a Git repository:

```{.bash .run-ci}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
git init
git status
```

`git init` creates a hidden `.git/` folder that holds the whole history.
`git status` is the command you will use most: it tells you what Git sees.

```text
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	.dockerignore
	.gitattributes
	.github/
	.gitignore
	CITATION.cff
	LICENSE
	README.md
	config/
	containers/
	data/
	...
```

### What is not listed, and why

Look carefully: the FASTQ files you downloaded in lesson 03 are missing. The
template's `.gitignore` tells Git to ignore them, and also files that do not
exist yet: software environments (`.pixi/`), results, rendered reports. Ask
Git why it ignores a path:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git check-ignore -v data/raw/fastq/SRR2584863_1.trim.sub.fastq .pixi/ results/vcf/SRR2584863_final_variants.vcf
```

```text
.gitignore:6:data/raw/**	data/raw/fastq/SRR2584863_1.trim.sub.fastq
.gitignore:2:.pixi/*	.pixi/
.gitignore:11:results/**	results/vcf/SRR2584863_final_variants.vcf
```

The rule of thumb: **commit what a person wrote; do not commit what a
program can rebuild or download.** Raw data is downloaded by
`scripts/download_data.py` (lesson 03); environments are rebuilt from
`pixi.lock` (lesson 05); results and reports are made by code. Git is also
not made for large files: the FASTQs alone are 350 MB. Large data belongs in
a data repository (Zenodo, or SRA and ENA for reads), with the script that
downloads it in Git. Tools such as Git LFS and DVC keep large files next to
the code; this course does not need them.

## 3. The first commit

A commit is a snapshot. Git works with three places:

- the **working copy**: the files in your folder, which you edit;
- the **staging area**: the changes you have chosen for the next commit;
- the **repository**: the history of commits, kept in `.git/`.

You **stage** changes with `git add`, then **commit** them with a message.
`git status` compares the three places: it lists changes not yet staged,
changes to be committed, and files Git does not track.

![Files move from the working copy (your folder) to the staging area with `git add`, and from there into the repository's history with `git commit`. Figure: Created by **Aziz Khan**, CC BY 4.0.](../assets/images/git/git-staging-local.png){fig-alt="Diagram: working copy, then 'stage changes' to the staging area, then 'commit changes' to the Git repository." width="80%"}

One file is still missing. The template includes a GitHub Action (step 9)
that rebuilds the project's software environment from a **lock file**, which
records the exact version of every package. Create it now; it takes a few
seconds and installs nothing (it prints the packages it recorded):

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
pixi lock
```

Lesson 05 explains what is in it. For now, the rule: `pixi.lock` is committed
together with `pixi.toml`, because together they say which software the code
ran with. The template's `.gitattributes` file tells Git how to treat some
files: `pixi.lock` is generated, so Git does not merge it line by line or
show it in diffs, and shell scripts keep Linux line endings, even on Windows.

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add .
git status
git commit -m "Create LTEE project with data download and metadata"
```

`git status` now lists every file under *Changes to be committed*, and the
commit prints its ID (yours differs) and a summary:

```text
[main (root-commit) 131b0d8] Create LTEE project with data download and metadata
 27 files changed, ...
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Good commit messages"}
Write the subject line in the imperative ("Add", "Fix", "Remove"), under
about 50 characters, with no full stop: *"Add GC content to read table"*. If
the change needs explaining, add a blank line and a body that says **what**
and **why** (the code already says how). A commit should be one logical
change: easy to describe, easy to undo.
:::

## 4. Change, inspect, commit

Add a sentence at the end of `README.md` that says what the project is for,
for example *"Practice project from the Reproducible and Open Science
lessons."* Use your editor, or append it from the terminal:

```{.bash .run-ci}
printf '\nPractice project from the Reproducible and Open Science lessons.\n' >> README.md
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git status
git diff
```

`git status` lists `README.md` under *Changes not staged for commit*.
`git diff` shows what changed since the last commit: `+` lines were added,
`-` lines removed. Here you see two `+` lines, an empty one and your
sentence. Stage the change and look again:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add README.md
git diff
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Say what the project is for in the README"
```

After `git add`, plain `git diff` shows nothing: the change has moved to the
staging area. `git diff --staged` shows what the next commit will contain.

### Stage only part of your work

Make two unrelated changes: a sentence in the metadata README, and a new file.

```{.bash .run-ci}
printf '\nThe reads were trimmed and subsampled by Data Carpentry.\n' >> metadata/README.md
printf 'Analysis notes for the LTEE project.\n' > docs/notes.md
git status
```

They belong in two commits. Stage and commit one at a time:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add metadata/README.md
git commit -m "Mention trimming and subsampling in the metadata"
git add docs/notes.md
git commit -m "Start analysis notes"
```

If you staged something by mistake, `git restore --staged FILE` takes it out
of the stage without changing the file. To stage only some of the changes
inside one file, `git add -p FILE` shows each change and asks whether to
stage it (`y` or `n`).

## 5. Browse the history

```{.bash .run-ci}
git log --oneline
git show --stat HEAD
git log --oneline -- metadata/README.md
```

```text
e30b49e Start analysis notes
7e0af94 Mention trimming and subsampling in the metadata
a119186 Say what the project is for in the README
131b0d8 Create LTEE project with data download and metadata
```

- `git log --oneline`: one line per commit, newest first. Each commit has an
  ID (a hash such as `e30b49e`; yours differ).
- `git show --stat HEAD`: what the latest commit changed. `HEAD` is Git's
  name for where you are now: the latest commit of the branch you are on.
  `HEAD~1` is the commit before it.
- `git log -- FILE`: only commits that touched that file.

Two more for later: `git log -p -- FILE` shows every change to a file as a
diff, and `git blame FILE` shows, for each line, the last commit that changed
it.

## 6. Put the project on GitHub

1. On GitHub, click **+** → **New repository**. Name it `ltee-project`,
   leave it **empty** (no README, no license, no `.gitignore`: you have them
   already), and choose Public or Private.


![Screenshot to create a new remote repository `ltee-project` on GitHub - https://github.com/new](../assets/images/git/create-new-repo.png){fig-alt="Diagram: Create New repository" width="90%"}

2. GitHub shows the commands to connect an existing repository. Use the SSH
   version, with your user name instead of `ada-lovelace`:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git remote add origin git@github.com:ada-lovelace/ltee-project.git
git push -u origin main
git remote -v
```

`origin` is the conventional name for "the copy on GitHub"; `git remote -v`
shows where it points. `-u` remembers it, so later you only type `git push`
and `git pull`. Reload the GitHub page: your files, your README and your
history are there, and the data is not.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="No SSH key? Use HTTPS and the GitHub CLI"}
Some networks block SSH, and some computers make keys hard to set up.
GitHub's command line tool, `gh`, can log you in through the browser
instead:

```{.bash .norun}
pixi global install gh
gh auth login
```

Answer *GitHub.com*, *HTTPS*, *Yes* (authenticate Git with your GitHub
credentials) and *Login with a web browser*. Then use the HTTPS address in
step 2:

```{.bash .norun}
git remote add origin https://github.com/ada-lovelace/ltee-project.git
git push -u origin main
```
:::

![Your local repository pushes commits to the remote repository and pulls (or fetches) others' commits from it; a collaborator's copy does the same. A clone starts a new local copy with the full history. Figure: By *Aziz Khan*, CC BY 4.0.](../assets/images/git/git-staging-remote.png){fig-alt="Diagram: a remote repository in the cloud; local repository A clones, pulls, fetches and pushes; a second local copy B does the same." width="80%"}

Every copy has the whole history. Four commands move commits between them:

- `git push` sends your new commits to the remote.
- `git clone URL` makes a new local copy, history included (*Try it
  yourself* 2).
- `git fetch` downloads the remote's new commits without changing your
  files; `git log --oneline --all` then shows them, on `origin/main`.
- `git pull` is a fetch followed by a merge into the branch you are on: it
  brings your copy up to date.

::: {.callout-note title="Private or public?"}
A course project can start private and become public when you publish (lesson
12). Either way, never commit passwords, tokens or personal data: removing
something from Git history later is hard.
:::

## 7. Branches

A branch is a separate line of work. You keep `main` working while you try
something on a branch, and merge it when it is ready.

![A branch is a label that points at a commit. While `add-fastqc` and `fix-ref-path` gain commits, `main` stays where it is. Each branch is merged back when its work is ready.](../assets/images/git/git-branches.svg){#fig-git-branches fig-alt="Two branches leave main, one above and one below. Each gains commits while main stays still, then merges back."}

Each dot in the figure is a commit. A branch is not a copy of your files: it
is a movable label that points at one commit, and `HEAD` follows the branch
you are on. `git switch -c add-fastqc` (1) puts a new label on the current
commit. Each commit you make (2) moves only that label forward, so `main`
stays untouched and keeps working while you experiment. When the change is
ready, a merge (3) brings it into `main`. On GitHub you do this through a
pull request, so a teammate can review it first.

Try it with a *decision log*, a file that records analysis choices and why
you made them. Make a branch:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch -c add-decision-log
```

Create `docs/decisions.md` in your editor with this content:

```{.markdown filename="docs/decisions.md" .write}
# Decision log

- Variant filter: minimum read depth 2 (the vcfutils.pl default, as in the Data Carpentry lesson).
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add docs/decisions.md
git commit -m "Start a decision log"
git log --oneline --graph --all
```

```text
* b66eaaa (HEAD -> add-decision-log) Start a decision log
* e30b49e (origin/main, main) Start analysis notes
* 7e0af94 Mention trimming and subsampling in the metadata
* a119186 Say what the project is for in the README
* 131b0d8 Create LTEE project with data download and metadata
```

Only the `add-decision-log` label moved; `main` (and `origin/main`, the last
state you pushed) still point at the commit before. Merge the branch into
`main` and delete it:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch main
git merge add-decision-log
git branch -d add-decision-log
```

```text
Updating e30b49e..b66eaaa
Fast-forward
 docs/decisions.md | 3 +++
```

*Fast-forward*: `main` had not moved since you made the branch, so Git only
moved the `main` label forward to your commit. The history stays one straight
line. When both branches have new commits, Git joins them with a *merge
commit*, as in the next step. (The figure draws every merge as a join,
because GitHub's **Merge pull request** button always makes a merge commit.)
`git branch -d` deletes only the label: the commit is now on `main`.

## 8. A merge conflict

When two branches change the same line differently, Git cannot decide for you.
Here two teammates, Ada and Ben, both change the depth threshold. You play
both of them, on your laptop; in a real team each would work on their own
computer, and the conflict would appear when the second one's work is merged.

The shortcut `git commit -am "MESSAGE"` stages every *tracked* file that
changed and commits it in one step. It does not add new files.

First Ada, on her branch:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch -c depth-5
```

In `docs/decisions.md`, change the filter line. The file is now:

```{.markdown filename="docs/decisions.md" .write}
# Decision log

- Variant filter: minimum read depth 5 (Ada: fewer false calls).
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git commit -am "Raise minimum depth to 5"
git switch main
git switch -c depth-10
```

Then Ben, on another branch that also starts from `main`, where the line
still says depth 2. Change it to his version:

```{.markdown filename="docs/decisions.md" .write}
# Decision log

- Variant filter: minimum read depth 10 (Ben: about the mean depth of these data).
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git commit -am "Raise minimum depth to 10"
git switch main
git merge depth-5
```

Ada's branch is a fast-forward: `main` now points at her commit. Ben's branch
started from the old `main` and changes the line Ada changed:

```{.bash .run-ci .expect-fail}
git merge depth-10
```

```text
Auto-merging docs/decisions.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in docs/decisions.md
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

Nothing is lost. If you want to stop and think, `git merge --abort` puts
everything back as it was before `git merge`. Otherwise, open the file. Git
has written both versions into it:

```text
# Decision log

<<<<<<< HEAD
- Variant filter: minimum read depth 5 (Ada: fewer false calls).
=======
- Variant filter: minimum read depth 10 (Ben: about the mean depth of these data).
>>>>>>> depth-10
```

Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is the version on the branch you are on
(`main`, with Ada's change); between `=======` and `>>>>>>> depth-10` is the
version from the branch you are merging. Resolve the conflict by writing the
version you agree on, **without the markers**. This is a scientific decision,
not a Git one: talk to Ben. Here the team keeps both thresholds for now,
because the question of the project is exactly which one to trust (lesson
09). Replace the whole file with:

```{.markdown filename="docs/decisions.md" .write}
# Decision log

- Variant filter: report results at minimum read depth 2 and 10, and decide which to keep
  once we can compare them (Ada wanted 5 to reduce false calls; Ben 10, about the mean depth).
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add docs/decisions.md
git commit -m "Resolve depth threshold: compare 2 and 10"
git log --oneline --graph -5
```

```text
*   15b653d (HEAD -> main) Resolve depth threshold: compare 2 and 10
|\
| * 74d8bd0 (depth-10) Raise minimum depth to 10
* | a943ec9 (depth-5) Raise minimum depth to 5
|/
* b66eaaa Start a decision log
* e30b49e (origin/main) Start analysis notes
```

This time both branches had new commits, so the resolution is a merge commit
with two parents: the history keeps both lines. Delete the merged branches and
push:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git branch -d depth-5 depth-10
git push
```

## 9. Pull requests and the Reproduce check

From now on, every lesson ends with a **branch and a pull request** (PR) on
GitHub, even if you work alone: it gives you a page that shows the change, a
place for comments, and automatic checks. This is how most open-source and lab
code is reviewed.

Start a branch and make a change on it: tell readers of the README how to get
the data (in your editor, or with the `printf` line below).

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch -c lesson-04-readme
printf '\n## Get the data\n\n    pixi exec python scripts/download_data.py\n' >> README.md
git commit -am "Say how to get the data in the README"
git push -u origin lesson-04-readme
```

Before you open the pull request, look at what GitHub will run on it. The
template put a workflow in `.github/workflows/reproduce.yml`:

```{.bash .run}
cat .github/workflows/reproduce.yml
```

On every push and pull request (`on:`), GitHub starts a fresh Linux machine
(`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`), clones your repository, rebuilds the environment
from `pixi.lock` (`locked: true` fails if the lock file is out of date), runs
`pixi run reproduce`, and checks that the run changed no committed file. For
now `reproduce` only prints *"Nothing to reproduce yet"*, so the check is
green but proves little. In lesson 05 you make it download the data and run
the pipeline on that fresh machine: then a green check means your project
reproduces from a clean clone.

Then, on GitHub:

1. Click **Compare & pull request**. Write what the change does and why, then
   **Create pull request**.
2. Look at the **Files changed** tab. In a team, a colleague reviews here.
3. Look at the checks: **Reproduce** runs. Click **Details** to read its log.
4. When the check is green, **Merge pull request**, then delete the branch.

With the GitHub CLI (step 6), `gh pr create --fill` does step 1 from the
terminal.

Back on your laptop, bring `main` up to date. `git pull` fetches the merge
commit GitHub made:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch main
git pull
```

Working without GitHub? Merge on your laptop instead. After a `git pull` this
changes nothing (Git says *Already up to date*):

```{.bash .run-ci}
git merge lesson-04-readme
git push
```

The branch is merged, so delete your copy of it. `git fetch --prune` also
removes `origin/lesson-04-readme`, the branch you deleted on GitHub:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git branch -d lesson-04-readme
git fetch --prune
```

## 10. Tags

A tag gives a commit a permanent name, for example the version you hand in or
the version behind a figure. The pull request is merged, so tag the state of
the project after this lesson. You will use tags for releases in lesson 12.

```{.bash .run-ci}
git tag -a lesson-04 -m "State of the project after lesson 04"
git push origin lesson-04
git tag -n
```

```text
lesson-04       State of the project after lesson 04
```

`-a` makes an *annotated* tag, which stores a message, an author and a date.
`git tag -n` lists the tags with their messages, and `git show lesson-04`
shows the tag and the commit it names.

## Try it yourself

1. Which commit last changed `docs/decisions.md`, and what did it say before?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   `git log --oneline -- docs/decisions.md` lists the commits; `git show
   HASH~1:docs/decisions.md` prints the file as it was one commit earlier
   (replace `HASH` with the commit ID).
   :::

2. Clone your repository into a new folder, as a colleague would, and check
   that the data is *not* there but can be downloaded.

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   ```{.bash .run-ci}
   cd ~/cbio7501
   git clone git@github.com:ada-lovelace/ltee-project.git ltee-project-clone
   ls ltee-project-clone/data/raw
   cd ltee-project-clone
   pixi exec python scripts/download_data.py --verify-only || echo "data not downloaded yet, as expected"
   cd ~/cbio7501 && rm -rf ltee-project-clone
   ```

   Only `README.md` is in `data/raw/`. `pixi exec python

   :::

## Break it: delete your work, then get it back

Disaster: you delete the download script and the sample sheet, and even
commit the deletion.

```{.bash .run-ci}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
git rm -q scripts/download_data.py metadata/samples.tsv
git commit -m "Clean up (oops)"
ls scripts metadata
```

The files are gone from the folder and from the latest commit. They are not
gone from history. Ask Git for the last commit that touched the script: it is
the commit that deleted it.

```{.bash .run-ci}
git log --oneline -1 -- scripts/download_data.py
```

```text
de58641 Clean up (oops)
```

The files are still in the commit before that one. `HASH~1` means "the commit
before HASH", so you could restore them from `de58641~1` (use your ID). Here
the deletion is also your latest commit, `HEAD`, so `HEAD~1` is the same
commit:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git restore --source=HEAD~1 scripts/download_data.py metadata/samples.tsv
git status --short
```

```text
?? metadata/samples.tsv
?? scripts/download_data.py
```

`??` means *untracked*: the files are back in your folder, but the latest
commit says they are deleted. Commit them again:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git add scripts/download_data.py metadata/samples.tsv
git commit -m "Restore download script and sample sheet"
```

Without Git, this was a lost afternoon (or a lost thesis). The only work Git
cannot give back is work you never committed, so commit small and often, and
push.

::: {.callout-warning}
`git restore FILE` (without `--staged`) throws away **uncommitted** changes to
`FILE`. Use it on purpose.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Going further: which undo?"}
| Situation | Command | What happens |
|-----------|---------|--------------|
| You changed a file and want the last committed version back | `git restore FILE` | the change is lost |
| You staged a change by mistake | `git restore --staged FILE` | the change leaves the stage and stays in the file |
| Uncommitted changes stop `git switch` or `git pull` | `git stash`, later `git stash pop` | the changes are put aside, then brought back |
| The last commit is wrong and not pushed yet | fix the files, `git add` them, then `git commit --amend` | the last commit is replaced (this also fixes its message) |
| A commit you already pushed was wrong | `git revert HASH` | a new commit undoes it; the history keeps both |
| A commit deleted a file | `git restore --source=HASH~1 FILE` | the *Break it* above |

Do not amend a commit you have pushed: GitHub would then have a commit your
copy no longer has, and your next push is rejected. Use `git revert` instead.
:::

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `Please tell me who you are` | Run the `git config --global` commands in step 1. |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` on push | Your SSH key is not set up or not added to GitHub: see [lesson 00](00-setup.qmd#git-and-github); test with `ssh -T git@github.com`. Or use the HTTPS route in step 6. |
| `Support for password authentication was removed` on push | GitHub does not take your password in the terminal. Use SSH, or `gh auth login` (step 6). |
| `error: src refspec main does not match any` | You have no commits yet, or your branch is called `master`: run `git branch` and push the name it shows. |
| `! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)` | GitHub has commits you do not have (for example a merged PR). Run `git pull`, then push again. |
| `fatal: not a git repository` | You are not in the project folder: `cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project`. |
| Git wants to commit `data/raw/...` or `.pixi/` | Your `.gitignore` is missing or was changed; compare with the template's. If already staged: `git rm -r --cached data/raw` (keeps the files on disk). |
| `CONFLICT (content)` and you are not ready to resolve it | `git merge --abort` puts everything back as it was before the merge. |
| `Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten` on `git switch` or `git pull` | Commit the changes first, or put them aside with `git stash` and bring them back with `git stash pop`. |
| `error: the branch '...' is not fully merged` after a pull request | The PR was merged with *Squash and merge* or *Rebase and merge*, which make new commits. Check on GitHub that it is merged, then delete the branch with `git branch -D`. |
| An editor opens with strange text after `git commit` or `git merge` | Git wants a message. In `vim`: type `:wq` and Enter. Set a friendlier editor with `git config --global core.editor "nano"`. |
| The Reproduce check fails with `lock file not up-to-date` | `pixi.lock` is missing or older than `pixi.toml`: run `pixi lock`, commit `pixi.lock`, push. |
| The Reproduce check fails on GitHub but works on your laptop | Something is on your laptop that is not in the repository. That is the point of the check: read its log. |

## Apply it to your own project

Put your own project under Git and on GitHub the same way: commit the data
download script, not the data, and open one pull request. The repository can
be private if your research is not public yet; add the instructor as a
collaborator. In lesson 05 you give
its `reproduce` task real work.

## Key points

- `git add` stages, `git commit` records a snapshot with a message; `git status`, `git diff` and `git diff --staged` tell you where you are.
- Commit what people write; ignore what programs download or rebuild (`.gitignore`).
- History lets you see any past version and restore deleted work, as long as it was committed.
- Branches are labels. A merge fast-forwards when only one side moved, and makes a merge commit when both did; conflicts are decisions you resolve by editing (or leave with `git merge --abort`).
- GitHub adds remotes, pull requests and Actions; the *Reproduce* check runs on every push and gets real work in lesson 05.
